10. Pipelines

Say you own the Monday report the sales team presents. It reads orders by city, which read the cleaned orders, which read the raw orders feed, and a bad row anywhere below ends up on their slides. Real pipelines are layered like that: cleaned tables feed joined tables feed reports. In sverify the layers are transforms composed directly, each piped from the one below, so the code reads in the order the data flows: orders.pipe(paid).pipe(doubled) is the same node as the call form doubled(paid(orders)). The other inputs of a layer come by keyword, as base.pipe(cities, customers=customers). Without a .write in between they fuse into one plan, maintained as one incremental view (chapter 9). .write(sink) stores a layer, as a cache in the middle of a job or as its output; the layers above read the stored table as a versioned source, through its change feed. So an intermediate result is computed once and shared, and only changes flow through the layers. This chapter brings chapters 8 and 9 together: the base layer is the contracted orders.pipe(paid).pipe(doubled), and its guarantees keep holding in every state of the pipeline, not only the first.

Three layers

data.text/markdown:
• paid and doubled have no .write between them, so they fuse into one plan; .write(DeltaSink(...)) stores the result as base. cities and located read base's Delta table, not orders.
  • A contracted transform piped from a stored node builds on what that node's plan proved, as in a direct composition: cities requires _.doubled.notnull() of base, which doubled guarantees, so it is checked once, when the node is built, and never on the data. A precondition base doesn't guarantee raises CompositionError right there.
  • sv.group(by_city, by_location) refreshes both reports against the same source versions; base is refreshed and written once for the two of them, upstream first. Its first refresh checked paid's preconditions on all of orders (the requires … (checked on data) lines above).
  • located is a left join, so it is recomputed and diffed on each refresh (chapter 9). Its change would still flow to any node reading it. status() says so:
cities: base@v2, customers@v0
located: base@v2, customers@v0; recomputed (not incrementally maintainable (left join, fetch or window))
base: orders@v0; stored in /tmp/tmpjqfg31mb/base

Changes, layer by layer

We'll feed the pipeline. Each button changes orders and customers and refreshes both reports. The first is valid; the other two each insert an order that breaks a precondition of paid. We refresh with audit=True, so every batch is also compared with recomputation before it is applied (AuditError otherwise).

data.text/markdown:
Why the guarantees survive every batch

Whoever reads base relies on its guarantees on the hundredth batch as much as on the first. paid's preconditions were checked on all of orders once, on the first refresh. After that, only the batch is checked:
  • row conditions (amount >= 0) on the inserted rows;
  • keys (unique(id)) among the inserted rows and against the keys of the rows the batch keeps.
That is enough, by theorem Spec.update in SubstraitLean/Compose.lean: a table's contract survives a batch if the inserted rows satisfy the row conditions and their keys clash with neither each other nor the kept rows. Triple.maintained then says a contracted view's guarantees hold in the new state. So base satisfies doubled ≥ 0 and is non-NULL after every batch, without ever re-checking the whole table, and the Delta table it is written to records those guarantees with every version, for the layers that read it. The layering itself is Rel.chain_sound (DBSP's chain rule): when a view reads another view's stored result, and gets that view's change as its change table (here, through the Delta change feed), its own update plan is still correct. For a recomputed view, ZSet.diff_correct shows new − old is a valid change to pass on. Each refresh brings the layers up to date upstream first and writes every stored node exactly once per state. If the job stops and restarts, building the same nodes again is enough: the first refresh resumes each stored node from its table when the plan and the source versions match, rather than computing it again.

Your own source and sink

Say the customers don't live in the lake at all. The CRM team gives you an API that returns the customers who signed up after a given time, and finance wants the city report as a Parquet file on their share, not as a Delta table. Neither needs a table format. A source you write is one method, read(since): it returns the rows that are new since the last read and a cursor to start from next time, as a Batch. A sink you write is one method too, write(change): it stores what a refresh hands it. sverify does the rest: it numbers the reads as versions, works out what changed, checks the preconditions, and decides when a state needs writing at all. We'll read the CRM with from_query, which builds a source from a function and the column to keep a high-water mark on, and write the report with a sink of our own that keeps the contract next to the file, so a restarted job knows what it already wrote.

console.name: stdout
console.text:
base:
  orders@v0: no new version
  view base: orders@v0
  wrote base from orders@v0: already committed (v2)
city_report:
  computed
  wrote city_report from base@v2, crm@v1: overwrite, 2 row(s) written, 0 deleted
base:
  orders@v0: no new version
  view base: orders@v0
  wrote base from orders@v0: already committed (v2)
city_report:
  base@v2: no new version
  crm@v1→v2: 1 insert(s), 0 delete(s); Δ trusted as rows appended to crm v1→v2, assuming rows only arrive with a greater signed_up
  view city_report: base@v2, crm@v2
  wrote city_report from base@v2, crm@v2: update, 1 row(s) written, 0 deleted

data.text/markdown: The first refresh read the CRM in full as version 1 and wrote the file; the second read only bob, as version 2. The report line says what that rests on: the rows were appended, assuming customers only arrive with a greater signed_up. That is the watermark job's assumption from chapter 1, and it can break: a sign-up the CRM records late, with an earlier time, falls below the cursor and is never read. We'll record one and refresh with audit=True, which reads the source again in full, up to the cursor, and compares it with what the batches built.

console.name: stdout
console.text:
base:
  orders@v0: no new version
  view base: orders@v0
  wrote base from orders@v0: already committed (v2)
city_report:
  base@v2: no new version
  crm@v2: no new version
  view city_report: base@v2, crm@v2
  wrote city_report from base@v2, crm@v2: already committed
AuditError: crm@v2 differs from the table read again in full: its batches missed rows; nothing was applied

data.text/markdown:
The plain refresh saw nothing new; the audit caught the row the cursor skipped, and applied nothing. A source you write can't promise more than its reads do, so be plain about it: give an assumes= that says what your batches rely on, and audit now and then. The rest of the toolkit, in sverify.io:
  • from_frame(fn) reads the whole table on every refresh and diffs it against the last read, so the change is exact and nothing is assumed; from_files(path) reads the files that are new in a directory. Subclass Source for anything else; a batch can also be a whole table (kind="snapshot") or rows added and removed (kind="changes").
  • A sink's write gets a SinkChange: the rows added and removed since its last write, or the whole table on the first, with the contract to record. committed() reads that contract back, so each state is written once even across restarts; leave it out and sverify remembers for the life of the process. sink_from(fn) hands the whole table to a function.
  • These sources have no metadata, so preconditions on them are checked on the rows, and they keep the table in memory. A restarted job reads them in full again, and numbers its versions above the ones its sinks recorded, so nothing is skipped by mistake. A table format with statistics and a change feed implements the full VersionedSource protocol instead, as Delta and Iceberg do.
  • Credentials stay out of your code: Storage holds object store options, or a function that fetches fresh ones, and is shared by every table that needs it.
You can now stack transforms into layers that pass only their changes along, store the ones others read, and rely on every contract's guarantees in every state while only the batch is checked, whether the data comes from a lake, an API or a folder of files. Next up, Engines and SQL runs the same checked plans on Polars and DataFusion, and as SQL for Snowflake and Spark.
